# 🦥 UNSLOTH — Recherche Complète et Détaillée

## 1. Qu'est-ce que Unsloth ?

**Unsloth** est un **framework open-source** (licence Apache-2.0) conçu pour **accélérer radicalement le fine-tuning** (entraînement spécialisé) et l'apprentissage par renforcement (RL) des **modèles de langage de grande taille (LLM)**.

Son objectif principal : résoudre les **bouteils computationnels** du fine-tuning de LLM — coût élevé et mémoire importante — en permettant l'entraînement de modèles qui nécessiteraient normalement du matériel d'entreprise, **sur du matériel grand public** (cartes graphiques consumer).

> ⚠️ **Remarque importante** : Unsloth a considérablement évolué. À l'origine (2023) c'était une **bibliothèque Python** pour le fine-tuning. Aujourd'hui (2026), c'est devenu une **application de bureau complète** pour exécuter et entraîner des modèles LLM et de diffusion (image, vidéo, audio).

---

## 2. Histoire et Fondateurs

| Élément | Détails |
|---|---|
| **Fondation** | 2023 |
| **Fondateurs** | **Daniel Han** et **Michael Han**, frères australiens |
| **Formation** | UNSW Australia (Sydney) |
| **Fond** | Daniel Han a un parcours technique (NVIDIA, FiscalNote) ; Michael Han est ingénieur produit et designer |
| **Statut** | **YC S24** (Startup Y Combinator saison 2024) |
| **Équipe** | ~10 personnes |
| **Usage** | Plus de **10 millions** d'utilisateurs (d'après les sources) |

Le nom vient de "Sloth" (le paresseux en anglais) — l'emblème est le **paresseux** 🦥.

---

## 3. Fonctionnalités Principales

### 🚀 Performance
- **Fine-tuning 2× plus rapide avec 70% de VRAM en moins**, sans perte de précision
- Sur GPU unique : jusqu'à **10× plus rapide** que Flash Attention 2
- En configuration multi-GPU : jusqu'à **30× plus rapide**
- 0% de dégradation de précision par rapport aux implémentations standards QLoRA

### 🧠 Types de modèles supportés
- **LLMs** : Qwen3.8, GLM-5.3-Flash, Kimi K3, MiniMax-H3, DeepSeek-V4, Gemma 4
- **Modèles de diffusion** : image, vidéo
- **TTS** (synthèse vocale)
- **Modèles d'embeddings**
- Formats : **GGUF, MLX, QAT, MTP**

### 🔧 Formats et déploiement
- Export vers **GGUF** (pour llama.cpp), **NVFP4, FP8**
- Compatibilité avec **vLLM, Ollama, llama.cpp**
- API compatible **OpenAI** et **Anthropic**

### 🤖 Agents et IA
- Intégration avec **Claude Code, Codex, DeepSeek Harness, Hermes, OpenCode, OpenClaw**
- Fonctionnalités **MCP**, **tool calling**, exécution de code
- **Recherche web** privée, **deep research**, **RAG**, window de contexte auto-compacting

### 🖥️ Formats d'installation
- **Unsloth Desktop** (app native) — recommandé
- **Unsloth Studio** (interface web)
- **Unsloth Core** (version par code)
- **Docker** (image `unsloth/unsloth`, version ROCm pour AMD `unsloth/unsloth-rocm`)

### 🌐 Plateformes supportées
- **Windows, Linux, WSL, macOS**
- GPUs : **NVIDIA, AMD, Intel**, CPU, backend **Vulkan**
- Configurations multi-GPU

---

## 4. Implémentation Technique

### 🔬 Custom Kernels (noyaux personnalisés)
Le cœur de l'optimisation repose sur des **Triton kernels manuscrits** — du code GPU écrit à la main qui remplace les modules PyTorch standards :

- **Matrices** : optimisées pour l'hardware NVIDIA
- **Attention** : calculs d'attention accélérés
- **Déquantification** : kernels de déquantification 4-bit rapides
- **Gradient** : calcul de gradient mémoire-efficient

### 📊 Quantification NF4 (NF4 = NormalFloat4)
- Allocation de **bins de quantification non uniformes** correspondant aux quantiles d'une distribution normale standard
- Prévient la perte d'information théorique lors de la compression en 4 bits

### ⚙️ Autres optimisations
- **Backpropagation manuellement dérivée**
- **Gradient checkpointing** optimisé (équilibre vitesse/mémoire)
- Réduction du stockage des **activations intermédiaires**

---

## 5. Méthodes d'Installation

### 📦 Unsloth Core (par code)
```bash
# Linux, WSL
curl -fsSL https://unsloth.ai/install.sh | sh

# macOS, Linux, WSL (uv)
uv venv unsloth_env --python 3.13
source unsloth_env/bin/activate
uv pip install unsloth --torch-backend=auto

# Windows
winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e
.\unsloth_env\Scripts\activate
uv pip install unsloth --torch-backend=auto
```

### 🐳 Docker
```bash
docker run -d --name unsloth --gpus all --ipc=host \
  -p 8000:8000 -p 8888:8888 \
  -v "$PWD":/workspace/host \
  -v "$HOME/.cache/huggingface":/workspace/.cache/huggingface \
  -v unsloth-studio:/opt/unsloth-studio \
  unsloth/unsloth
```

### 🖥️ Desktop
Téléchargement direct depuis les releases GitHub (Windows `.exe`, macOS `.dmg`, Linux `.deb`/`.AppImage`).

---

## 6. Méthodes d'Entraînement Supportées

### 📚 Supervisé (SFT)
- Fine-tuning complet
- Entraînement **4-bit, 8-bit, 16-bit**
- **LoRA** et **QLoRA** (optimisés jusqu'à 2.7× plus rapides, 74% de VRAM de moins)

### 🎯 LoRA / QLoRA
Appliqué par défaut aux couches **attention et MLP**, avec gestion automatique de la mémoire.

### 🔁 Apprentissage par renforcement (RL)
- **GRPO** (Group Relative Policy Optimization) — l'algorithme de DeepSeek pour R1
- **PPO** (Proxible Policy Optimization)
- **Online DPO**, **Reward modeling**
- **GSPO, DrGRPO, DAPO, FP8**

> **GRPO** est particulièrement novateur : il **supprime le besoin de modèles de récompense et de valeur séparés** (contrairement au PPO), ce qui économise énormément de mémoire et accélère l'entraînement.

---

## 7. Performances et Benchmarks

| Métrique | Résultat |
|---|---|
| **Vitesse (GPU unique)** | Jusqu'à 10× vs Flash Attention 2 |
| **Vitesse (multi-GPU)** | Jusqu'à 30× |
| **Réduction mémoire** | Jusqu'à 70-74% |
| **Précision** | 0% de dégradation |
| **Validation** | Benchmarking par Hugging Face sur **59 runs**, 4 datasets (Tesla T4, A100) |

**Exemples concrets :**
- Fine-tuning **Llama 3.1 3B** : seulement **9 Go de VRAM** (vs 30+ Go standard)
- **70B** : entraînable sur un GPU de 48 Go
- **405B** : entraînable sur multi-GPU
- Contexte ultra-long : jusqu'à **500K+** tokens sur un seul GPU

---

## 8. Modèles Supportés

| Famille | Support |
|---|---|
| **Llama** | 1B à 405B |
| **Mistral** | ✅ |
| **Qwen** | ✅ (Qwen3.8) |
| **DeepSeek** | ✅ (DeepSeek-V4) |
| **Gemma** | ✅ (Gemma 4) |
| **Phi** | ✅ |
| **GPT** | ✅ |
| **GLM** | ✅ (GLM-5.2, 5.3-Flash) |
| **Modèles de diffusion** | Image, vidéo |

---

## 9. Avantages et Inconvénients

### ✅ Points forts
- **Accès démocratisé** à l'entraînement de LLM sur matériel grand public
- **Open-source** et gratuit
- **Documentation** et **notebooks** gratuits abondants
- Support de nombreux formats de déploiement
- Écosystème Hugging Face intégré

### ⚠️ Points à considérer
- Optimisations principalement orientées **NVIDIA** (certaines fonctions comme ROCm nécessitent Linux natif)
- Surface d'installation étendue (Desktop/Studio/Core) qui peut être complexe
- Certains extras (LAN/HTTPS) activés par défaut → **sécurité à surveiller**

---

## 10. Ressources Utiles

- **GitHub** : github.com/unslothai/unsloth
- **Site officiel** : unsloth.ai
- **Documentation** : unsloth.ai/docs
- **Twitter/X** : @UnslothAI
- **Discord** : discord.gg/unsloth
- **Reddit** : reddit.com/r/unsloth
- **Docker** : hub.docker.com/r/unsloth/unsloth

---

## 📌 Conclusion

**Unsloth** est devenu l'un des outils les plus influents pour le **fine-tuning local de LLM**. Grâce à ses **custom kernels Triton**, sa **quantification NF4** et ses **optimisations mémoire**, il permet d'entraîner des modèles de 405B paramètres sur du matériel consumer. Son évolution vers une **application de bureau complète** (Desktop/Studio/Core) avec support multi-modale (image, vidéo, audio) et multi-plateforme (NVIDIA, AMD, Intel) en fait un écosystème complet pour le développement d'IA.

---

[Read guide.](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/install/docker) #### Community: - [Discord](https://discord.gg/unsloth) - [𝕏 (Twitter)](https://x.com/UnslothAI) - [Reddit](https://reddit.com/r/unsloth) ## ⭐ Features Unsloth works on **Windows, Linux, WSL** and **macOS**. We support **Multi GPU setups, NVIDIA, AMD, Intel GPUs, CPUs** and the **Vulkan** backend. ### Run & Build with AI * Run and train LLMs, MLX, GGUF, diffusion, embedding, audio models: [Qwen3.8](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/qwen3.8), [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/glm-5.3-flash), [Kimi K3](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/kimi-k3), MiniMax-H3, [DeepSeek-V4](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/deepseek-v4), [Gemma 4](https://unsloth.ai/docs/models/gemma-4). * **Agents & Tools:** Use local models with [Claude Code](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/claude-code), [Codex](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/codex), and [MCP](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/mcp), including tool calling and code execution. * **Search & RAG:** Use private and unlimited web search, deep research, auto-compaction (rolling context window) and RAG. * **Image and video:** Run and train [image](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/diffusion-image) and video diffusion or multimodal models * **Remote & LAN:** Access your local models from any device on [LAN](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/lan) or remotely through secure [Cloudflare](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/how-to-serve-local-llms-anywhere-secure-remote-access-with-cloudflare-and-unsloth) HTTPS. * **Connect:** Serve models through an [OpenAI compatible API](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/api). Also connect your ChatGPT/Codex subscription and [cloud providers](https://unsloth.ai/docs/integrations/connections) ### Train & Deploy * **Fine-tuning:** Train LLMs, diffusion, TTS, and embedding models 2× faster with 70% less VRAM with [no accuracy loss](https://unsloth.ai/blog#training) * **Complete support:** Supports [reinforcement learning](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide), LoRA, QLoRA, full fine tuning, pretraining, RL, GRPO, DPO, and FP8. * **Export & Deploy:** [Export](https://unsloth.ai/docs/new/studio/export) or Deploy models with including [GGUF](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/inference-and-deployment/saving-to-gguf), NVFP4, FP8 and more formats. * **Datasets:** Build datasets from PDFs, CSVs, DOCX files, and more with [Data Recipes](https://unsloth.ai/docs/new/studio/data-recipe). ## 🚀 Unsloth Start [Unsloth Start](https://unsloth.ai/docs/integrations/unsloth-start) connects [Claude Code](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/claude-code), [Codex](https://unsloth.ai/docs/basics/codex) and other agents to local models with one command. ```bash unsloth start claude --model unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:UD-Q4_K_XL ``` | Agent | Command | | --- | --- | | Claude Code | `unsloth start claude` | | OpenAI Codex | `unsloth start codex` | | DeepSeek Harness | `unsloth start dsh` | | Hermes Agent | `unsloth start hermes` | | OpenCode | `unsloth start opencode` | | OpenClaw | `unsloth start openclaw` | ## 📥 Install Unsloth can be used in three ways: **[Unsloth Desktop](https://unsloth.ai/download)**, the desktop app; **[Unsloth Studio](https://unsloth.ai/docs/new/studio/)**, the web UI; or **Unsloth Core**, the code based version. ### Unsloth Desktop (recommended)

### Unsloth Studio (web UI) #### macOS, Linux, WSL: ```bash curl -fsSL https://unsloth.ai/install.sh | sh ``` #### Windows: ```powershell irm https://unsloth.ai/install.ps1 | iex ``` #### Launch ```bash unsloth studio ``` #### HTTP Secure Deployment ```bash unsloth studio --secure ``` #### Docker Use our [Docker image](https://hub.docker.com/r/unsloth/unsloth) ```unsloth/unsloth```. On Linux, set up GPU access once with `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/unslothai/unsloth/main/docker/install_nvidia_toolkit.sh -o install_nvidia_toolkit.sh && sudo -E bash install_nvidia_toolkit.sh` (Windows: [Docker Desktop with WSL 2](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/install/docker)). **Linux / WSL (Bash):** ```bash # use -e UNSLOTH_STUDIO_SECURE=1 instead of -p 8000:8000 for a public Cloudflare HTTPS link docker run -d --name unsloth --gpus all --ipc=host \ -p 8000:8000 -p 8888:8888 \ -v "$PWD":/workspace/host \ -v "$HOME/.cache/huggingface":/workspace/.cache/huggingface \ -v unsloth-studio:/opt/unsloth-studio \ unsloth/unsloth && docker logs -f unsloth ``` The log ends with your links and a generated JupyterLab password, plus a generated Unsloth Studio password on the first run against a new `unsloth-studio` volume; change that one on first sign-in or Unsloth Studio stops after an hour. A reused volume keeps the password already stored on it, and `docker exec unsloth unsloth studio reset-password --username unsloth` mints a new one and prints it. Ctrl-C stops following the log, not the container; `docker rm -f unsloth` deletes it. The Hugging Face cache keeps your models and the `unsloth-studio` volume keeps your accounts, chats and trained models, both across `docker rm`; a volume from an older image is migrated on first start, its old code kept under `.unsloth-studio-legacy/`. Those ports publish on every interface: on a cloud host add `-e UNSLOTH_STUDIO_SECURE=1`, drop `-p 8000:8000` and bind JupyterLab to `-p 127.0.0.1:8888:8888`, or bind both to `127.0.0.1` and use an SSH tunnel. Tags (`unsloth/unsloth:core` for notebooks only), GPU support and options: [Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/r/unsloth/unsloth). On AMD there is a separate image, [`unsloth/unsloth-rocm`](https://hub.docker.com/r/unsloth/unsloth-rocm), with the run command and the supported cards on its [Docker Hub page](https://hub.docker.com/r/unsloth/unsloth-rocm). It carries the training stack only, so there is no Unsloth Studio or JupyterLab in it, and it needs native Linux: WSL exposes `/dev/dxg` rather than the `/dev/kfd` that ROCm needs. #### Remote HTTPS & LAN Access Server-side tools are on by default - so **be careful**! Keep your password safe, or use `--disable-tools` when exposing Unsloth. **Global HTTPS Access**: Creates a free Cloudflare link that serves Unsloth - you can access the link globally (even on your phone!) ```bash unsloth studio --secure ``` `-H 0.0.0.0` and different ports also work: ```bash unsloth studio -H 0.0.0.0 -p 8888 ``` **LAN Access (home network)**: `Settings > API keys > LAN access` #### Password management & headless starts Exposing Unsloth (`--secure`, `--cloudflare`, or a non-loopback `-H`) asks once at the terminal for a new admin password. Ctrl+C there aborts the launch rather than exposing the auto-generated one; set a password non-interactively instead, or use `-H 127.0.0.1` to stay off the network. On a non-loopback `-H` bind a terminal nobody answers is not a refusal: after ~30s Unsloth starts anyway and shuts down on the bootstrap deadline, so detached launches (`docker run -dt`, `tmux new -d`) are unaffected. ## What is Unsloth?

Unsloth is an open-source framework designed to dramatically accelerate the [fine](https://artificial-intelligence-wiki.com/ai-development/training-and-fine-tuning/fsdp-fine-tuning-guide/)-tuning and reinforcement learning of large language models. Developed to address the computational bottlenecks in LLM training, Unsloth achieves remarkable performance improvements through custom kernel implementations and memory optimizations.

The framework stands out in the crowded field of LLM training tools by delivering 2x faster training speeds with 70% less VRAM usage compared to standard methods like Flash Attention 2, all while maintaining zero accuracy loss. This makes it possible to [fine](https://artificial-intelligence-wiki.com/ai-development/training-and-fine-tuning/multilingual-fine-tuning/)-tune large models on consumer-grade GPUs that would otherwise require enterprise hardware.

Unsloth supports a comprehensive range of training methodologies including full [fine](https://artificial-intelligence-wiki.com/ai-development/training-and-fine-tuning/modal-fine-tuning-guide/)-tuning, LoRA, QLoRA, and various reinforcement learning algorithms. It works seamlessly with popular models from Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, and more, handling everything from small 1B parameter models to massive 405B parameter models.

What sets Unsloth apart is its versatility in model types. Beyond standard language models, it supports vision models, text-to-speech models, embedding models, and multimodal architectures. This comprehensive support combined with beginner-friendly notebooks and extensive documentation makes it accessible to both researchers and practitioners.

The framework integrates naturally with the Hugging Face ecosystem, working alongside popular libraries like Transformers and TRL (Transformer Reinforcement Learning). This integration allows developers to leverage existing workflows while gaining substantial performance improvements simply by incorporating Unsloth into their training pipeline.

## Key Features and Capabilities

Unsloth offers a comprehensive suite of features that make it the go-to solution for efficient LLM training in 2025. The framework's capabilities span performance optimizations, training methodologies, and extensive model support.

### Performance Optimizations

The core strength of Unsloth lies in its performance optimizations. On single GPU systems, Unsloth delivers 10x faster training compared to Flash Attention 2, with speedups reaching 30x on multi-GPU configurations. These improvements come from manually derived backpropagation steps and custom Triton kernels that replace standard PyTorch modules.

Memory usage is reduced by up to 70%, enabling training scenarios previously impossible on consumer hardware. You can [fine](https://artificial-intelligence-wiki.com/ai-development/rag-systems/rag-vs-fine-tuning/)-tune a Llama 3.1 3B model using only 9GB of VRAM, or train models with over 500K context length on a single GPU. The framework supports training on NVIDIA GPUs from Tesla T4 to H100, with portability to AMD and Intel GPUs.

Unsloth's optimizations maintain perfect accuracy with 0% degradation compared to standard QLoRA implementations. No approximations are made in the optimized code, ensuring that speed improvements don't compromise model quality. Benchmarking conducted by Hugging Face across 59 runs confirmed these claims with consistent results.

### Training Methods Supported

Unsloth supports the full spectrum of modern LLM training methodologies. For supervised [fine](https://artificial-intelligence-wiki.com/ai-development/rag-systems/fine-tuning-embeddings/)-tuning, it handles full fine-tuning, 4-bit training, 8-bit training, and 16-bit training across all model architectures. LoRA and QLoRA implementations are optimized for maximum efficiency while maintaining compatibility with standard implementations.

The framework is the most efficient reinforcement learning library available, using 80% less VRAM than alternatives. It supports GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), the algorithm used by DeepSeek to train their R1 reasoning models. Other supported RL methods include GSPO, FP8 training, DrGRPO, DAPO, PPO, reward modeling, and online DPO.

GRPO is particularly notable because it eliminates the need for separate reward and value models required by PPO, saving substantial memory and accelerating training. This efficiency makes it possible to perform reinforcement learning on hardware that couldn't handle traditional PPO implementations.

### Model Support

Unsloth is the only training framework that comprehensively supports vision models, text-to-speech models, embedding models, and reinforcement learning models while remaining fully customizable. It works with all major model families including Llama (1B to 405B), Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma, Phi, and GPT models.

The framework provides flexible chat templates and dataset formatting options, making it easy to adapt to different model architectures and training data formats. Ready-to-use notebooks are available for most popular models, providing starting points that can be customized for specific use cases.

Model deployment is streamlined with native support for llama.cpp, Ollama, and vLLM formats. After training, models can be directly converted and deployed using these popular inference engines, eliminating friction in the development-to-production pipeline.

## Installation and Setup

Getting started with Unsloth is straightforward, with multiple installation options to suit different development environments and use cases.

### Standard Installation

For most users, standard pip installation is the recommended approach. The basic installation command integrates Unsloth with PyTorch and the Hugging Face ecosystem:

```
pip install unsloth
```

For Windows users with PyTorch already installed, the installation process automatically detects the environment and configures accordingly. The framework supports the latest hardware including RTX 50x series, NVIDIA B200, and professional 6000-series GPUs.

After installation, you can verify the setup by importing Unsloth in Python and checking the version. The installation includes all necessary dependencies for basic fine-tuning operations, with additional packages automatically installed as needed for specific features like reinforcement learning or vision model training.

### Docker Setup

For production environments or to avoid dependency conflicts, Unsloth provides pre-built Docker containers with all dependencies configured. This option is ideal for teams wanting instant setup with no configuration required.

The Docker images include CUDA drivers, PyTorch, Transformers, TRL, and all Unsloth optimizations pre-configured for maximum performance. Simply pull the image and start training immediately without worrying about driver versions, CUDA compatibility, or library conflicts.

Container-based deployment also simplifies scaling to cloud environments or multi-node clusters. The same Docker image can run on local workstations, cloud instances, or Kubernetes clusters, ensuring consistency across development and production environments.

## Fine-Tuning with Unsloth

Fine-tuning LLMs with Unsloth follows a streamlined workflow that balances simplicity with powerful customization options. The framework's beginner-friendly approach makes it accessible while providing the flexibility experts need.

### Basic Fine-Tuning Workflow

The basic fine-tuning workflow in Unsloth consists of four main steps: model loading, dataset preparation, training configuration, and model saving. Start by loading a base model using Unsloth's FastLanguageModel class, which automatically applies memory optimizations.

Dataset preparation involves formatting your training data according to the model's chat template. Unsloth provides utilities to handle common formats like ShareGPT, Alpaca, and custom formats. The framework automatically handles tokenization and batching for optimal performance.

Training configuration uses familiar Hugging Face TrainingArguments, with Unsloth automatically optimizing parameters for your hardware. Specify your desired learning rate, batch size, and training duration, and Unsloth handles memory management and gradient accumulation automatically.

After training completes, save your model in multiple formats simultaneously. Unsloth can export to standard Hugging Face format, merge LoRA adapters into base models, convert to GGUF for llama.cpp, or prepare for vLLM deployment in a single operation.

### LoRA and QLoRA Training

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) and QLoRA (Quantized LoRA) training are fully optimized in Unsloth with custom kernels that dramatically accelerate adapter training. When using LoRA, specify the rank, alpha value, and target modules, and Unsloth handles the rest with optimal memory management.

QLoRA training in Unsloth uses 4-bit quantization to further reduce memory requirements without accuracy loss. This enables fine-tuning of 70B parameter models on consumer GPUs with 24GB VRAM, or even 13B models on GPUs with just 8GB VRAM.

The framework applies LoRA to attention and MLP layers by default, with options to customize which layers receive adapters. Gradient checkpointing is automatically configured based on available memory, balancing speed and memory usage for optimal training efficiency.

Benchmarking shows Unsloth's LoRA implementation is up to 2.7x faster than standard Transformers with integrated SDPA, using up to 74% less memory. These improvements scale across model sizes, making LoRA training practical even on limited hardware.

## Reinforcement Learning with Unsloth

Unsloth has emerged as the most efficient framework for reinforcement learning with LLMs, supporting cutting-edge algorithms like GRPO alongside traditional methods like PPO. The framework's RL capabilities use 80% less VRAM than alternatives, democratizing access to advanced training techniques.

### GRPO Training

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) represents a breakthrough in efficient reinforcement learning for LLMs. Developed by DeepSeek for training their R1 reasoning models, GRPO eliminates the need for separate reward and value models required by traditional PPO.

By removing these auxiliary models, GRPO saves massive amounts of memory and dramatically accelerates training. This efficiency makes it possible to perform RL training on hardware that couldn't support PPO, opening reinforcement learning to a much wider audience.

Unsloth's GRPO implementation includes support for FP8 training, matching the capabilities used in DeepSeek-R1. Ultra-long context RL is also supported, enabling training with context windows up to 380K tokens. This makes it possible to train models on entire codebases, long documents, or extended conversations.

The framework provides ready-to-use notebooks demonstrating GRPO training on various model sizes and tasks. These notebooks cover everything from reward function design to hyperparameter tuning, making it straightforward to implement GRPO for custom use cases.

### Other RL Methods

Beyond GRPO, Unsloth supports a comprehensive suite of reinforcement learning algorithms. PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) remains available for users who prefer established methods, with Unsloth optimizations making it significantly more efficient than standard implementations.

Online DPO (Direct Preference Optimization) provides an alternative to RL that often achieves comparable results with simpler setup. Unsloth's implementation handles the complexity of online preference collection while maintaining the performance benefits of its optimization engine.

Reward modeling is fully supported for cases where you need custom reward functions beyond simple classification. The framework handles the training of reward models with the same efficiency as policy training, and integrates seamlessly with both GRPO and PPO workflows.

Additional algorithms like GSPO, DrGRPO, and DAPO provide options for specialized use cases. The flexibility to switch between algorithms while maintaining consistent performance characteristics lets researchers experiment with different approaches without rewriting training code.

## Performance Benchmarks

Extensive benchmarking validates Unsloth's performance claims across diverse hardware configurations and model architectures. Independent testing by Hugging Face and NVIDIA confirms the framework's substantial advantages over standard training methods.

### Speed Comparisons

Testing against the latest Transformers version (4.36) with SDPA natively integrated shows Unsloth achieving up to 2.7x faster training speeds. On single GPU systems, speedups of 10x compared to Flash Attention 2 are common, with multi-GPU setups reaching 30x improvements.

Benchmarking was conducted across 59 runs using 4 different datasets on Tesla T4 and A100 Google Colab instances. QLoRA was applied to all linear layers with rank 16 and gradient checkpointing enabled, representing realistic training configurations.

The speedups remain consistent across model sizes. Training Llama 3.1 3B achieves 2x faster throughput, while larger 70B models see similar or greater improvements. This scaling ensures that benefits apply whether you're fine-tuning small specialized models or large general-purpose ones.

Hugging Face's independent benchmarking confirmed these results, adding credibility to performance claims. The consistent improvements across different testing environments and configurations demonstrate that Unsloth's optimizations are robust and reliable.

### Memory Efficiency

Memory usage reductions of up to 74% make previously impossible training scenarios practical on consumer hardware. Fine-tuning Llama 3.1 3B requires only 9GB of VRAM with Unsloth, compared to 30GB+ with standard methods. This brings 3B model training to GPUs like the RTX 3060 or RTX 4060 Ti.

For larger models, the efficiency gains are even more dramatic. 70B parameter models can be fine-tuned on single 48GB GPUs, and even 405B models become trainable on multi-GPU setups that would previously require dedicated ML clusters.

The memory savings come from multiple optimizations working together. Custom kernels reduce intermediate activation storage, gradient checkpointing is optimized for minimal overhead, and quantization is implemented efficiently without the accuracy penalties of naive approaches.

# 🎓 Tutoriel Pratique : Fine-Tuning d'un LLM avec Unsloth

## 📋 Prérequis

Avant de commencer, assurez-vous d'avoir :

|---|---|
| **GPU NVIDIA** | RTX 3060 (12 Go) ou mieux (12–24 Go de VRAM) |
| **RAM système** | 16 Go minimum |
| **Espace disque** | 20 Go |
| **Système** | Linux, WSL2, ou Windows |
| **Langage** | Python 3.13 |

> 💡 **Conseil débutant** : Commencez avec un petit modèle instruct comme **Llama 3.1 (8B)** ou un modèle encore plus petit (3B) pour tester rapidement.

---

## 🚀 ÉTAPE 1 — Installation

Choisissez votre méthode :

### Option A : Via pip (recommandé)
```bash
# Installer Python 3.13 et uv (gestionnaire de paquets rapide)
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
uv venv unsloth_env --python 3.13
source unsloth_env/bin/activate

# Installer Unsloth
uv pip install unsloth --torch-backend=auto
```

### Option B : Vérifier l'installation
```python
import unsloth
print(unsloth.__version__)
```

---

## 🎯 ÉTAPE 2 — Choisir le Modèle

Pour ce tutoriel, on fine-tune un modèle **Qwen3.8 (7B)** en **QLoRA** (4-bit) :

```python
model = unsloth.load_model(
    "unsloth/qwen3.8-7b-unsloth-bnb-4bit",
    max_seq_length=2048,          # Longueur de contexte (2048 recommandé pour tester)
    dtype=None,                   # None = auto-détecte le format
    load_in_4bit=True,            # Active QLoRA (4-bit) — économise 4× de mémoire
)
```

### 📌 Noms de modèles — Guide des suffixes
| Suffixe | Signification |
|---|---|
| `unsloth-bnb-4bit` | Quantification 4-bit dynamique Unsloth (meilleure précision) |
| `bnb-4bit` | Quantification 4-bit standard BitsAndBytes |
| *(aucun suffixe)* | Format original 16-bit ou 8-bit |

> ⚠️ **À ne pas faire** : Ne sautez pas directement au **fine-tuning complet (FFT)**. Commencez toujours par LoRA/QLoRA.

---

## 📊 ÉTAPE 3 — Préparer l'Ensemble de Données

Créez un fichier `dataset.py` avec vos données d'entraînement :

```python

    {"instruction": "Expliquez la photosynthèse.",
     "input": "",
     "output": "La photosynthèse est le processus par lequel les plantes convertissent la lumière en énergie."},

]

dataset = make_chat_template(dataset)
```

---

## 🔥 ÉTAPE 4 — Configurer et Lancer l'Entraînement

```python
from trl import SFTTrainer
from transformers import TrainingArguments

# Configuration de l'entraînement
trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    train_dataset=dataset,
    dataset_text_field="content",
    max_seq_length=2048,
    dataset_num_proc=2,
    tokenizer=model.tokenizer,
)

# Arguments d'entraînement (hyperparamètres)

    output_dir="outputs/qwen3.8-finetuned",
    report_to="none",                          # Désactive le suivi externe
    per_device_train_batch_size=2,             # Taille de lot par GPU
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,             # Simule un batch plus grand
    warmup_steps=5,
    num_train_epochs=3,                        # 1-3 époques recommandées
    learning_rate=2e-4,                        # Taux d'apprentissage

    optim="adamw_8bit",                        # Optimiseur mémoire-efficient
    gradient_checkpointing=True,               # Économise la mémoire
    bf16=True,                                 # BF16 si le GPU le supporte
    max_grad_norm=0.01,

trainer.train(trainer_args)
```

|---|---|

| **Ne descend pas** | ⚠️ Ajustez les hyperparamètres |
| **Tend vers 0** | ⚠️ Risque de *surapprentissage* (overfitting) — vérifiez la validation |

```python

```

For the complete documentation index, see [llms.txt](https://unsloth.ai/docs/llms.txt). This page is also available as [Markdown](https://unsloth.ai/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide.md).

# 🧬Fine-tuning LLMs Guide

Learn all the basics and best practices of fine-tuning. Beginner-friendly.

## 1. What Is Fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning / training / post-training models customizes its behavior, enhances + injects knowledge, and optimizes performance for domains and specific tasks. For example:

*

OpenAI’s **GPT-5** was post-trained to improve instruction following and helpful chat behavior.

*

The standard method of post training is called Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). Other methods include preference optimization (DPO, ORPO), distillation and [Reinforcement Learning (RL)](/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide) (GRPO, GSPO), where an "agent" learns to make decisions by interacting with an environment and receiving **feedback** in the form of **rewards** or **penalties**.

With [Unsloth](https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth), you can fine-tune or do RL for free on Colab, Kaggle, or locally with just 3GB VRAM by using our [notebooks](https://docs.unsloth.ai/get-started/unsloth-notebooks). By fine-tuning a pre-trained model on a dataset, you can:

*

**Update + Learn New Knowledge**: Inject and learn new domain-specific information.

*

**Customize Behavior**: Adjust the model’s tone, personality, or response style.

*

**Optimize for Tasks**: Improve accuracy and relevance for specific use cases.

**Example fine-tuning or RL use-cases**:

*

Enables LLMs to predict if a headline impacts a company positively or negatively.

*

Can use historical customer interactions for more accurate and custom responses.

*

Fine-tune LLM on legal texts for contract analysis, case law research, and compliance.

You can think of a fine-tuned model as a specialized agent designed to do specific tasks more effectively and efficiently. **Fine-tuning can replicate all of RAG's capabilities**, but not vice versa.

#### ❓What is LoRA/QLoRA?

In LLMs, we have model weights. Llama 70B has 70 billion numbers. Instead of changing all 70B numbers, we instead add thin matrices A and B to each weight, and optimize those. This means we only optimize 1% of weights. LoRA is when the original model is 16-bit unquantized while QLoRA quantizes to 4-bit to save 75% memory.

Instead of optimizing Model Weights (yellow), we optimize 2 thin matrices A and B.

#### Fine-tuning misconceptions:

You may have heard that fine-tuning does not make a model learn new knowledge or RAG performs better than fine-tuning. That is **false**. You can train a specialized coding model with fine-tuning and RL while RAG can’t change the model’s weights and only augments what the model sees at inference time. Read more FAQ + misconceptions [here](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-for-beginners/faq-+-is-fine-tuning-right-for-me#fine-tuning-vs.-rag-whats-the-difference):

[🤔FAQ + Is Fine-tuning Right For Me?](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-for-beginners/faq-+-is-fine-tuning-right-for-me)

> [**Introducing Unsloth Studio:**](/docs/new/studio) Our new open-source web UI for training and running models. This means you can now fine-tune models with no-code and have observability and automatic dataset creation features.

## 2. Choose the Right Model + Method

If you're a beginner, it is best to start with a small instruct model like Llama 3.1 (8B) and experiment from there. You'll also need to decide between normal fine-tuning, RL, QLoRA or LoRA training:

*

**Reinforcement Learning (RL) ** is used when you need a model to excel at a specific behavior (e.g., tool-calling) using an environment and reward function rather than labeled data. We have several [notebook examples](/docs/get-started/unsloth-notebooks#grpo-reasoning-rl-notebooks), but for most use-cases, standard SFT is sufficient.

*

**LoRA** is a parameter efficient training method that typically keeps the base model’s weights frozen and trains a small set of added low-rank adapter weights (in 16-bit precision).

*

**QLoRA** combines LoRA with 4-bit precision to handle very large models with minimal resources.

*

Unsloth also supports full fine-tuning (FFT) and pretraining, which require significantly more resources, but FFT is usually unnecessary. When done correctly, LoRA can match FFT.

*

Unsloth **all types models**: [text-to-speech](/docs/basics/text-to-speech-tts-fine-tuning), [embedding](/docs/basics/embedding-finetuning), GRPO, RL, [vision](/docs/basics/vision-fine-tuning), multimodal and more.

Research shows that **training and serving in the same precision** helps preserve accuracy. This means if you want to serve in 4-bit, train in 4-bit and vice versa.

We recommend starting with QLoRA, as it is one of the most accessible and effective methods for training models. Our [dynamic 4-bit](https://unsloth.ai/blog/dynamic-4bit) quants, the accuracy loss for QLoRA compared to LoRA is now largely recovered.

You can change the model name to whichever model you like by matching it with model's name on Hugging Face e.g. '`unsloth/llama-3.1-8b-unsloth-bnb-4bit`'.

We recommend starting with **Instruct models**, as they allow direct fine-tuning using conversational chat templates (ChatML, ShareGPT etc.) and require less data compared to **Base models** (which uses Alpaca, Vicuna etc). Learn more about the differences between [instruct and base models here](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/what-model-should-i-use#instruct-or-base-model).

*

Model names ending in `**unsloth-bnb-4bit**` indicate they are [**Unsloth dynamic 4-bit**](https://unsloth.ai/blog/dynamic-4bit) **quants**. These models consume slightly more VRAM than standard BitsAndBytes 4-bit models but offer significantly higher accuracy.

*

If a model name ends with just `**bnb-4bit**`, without "unsloth", it refers to a standard BitsAndBytes 4-bit quantization.

*

Models with **no suffix** are in their original **16-bit or 8-bit formats**. While they are the original models from the official model creators, we sometimes include important fixes - such as chat template or tokenizer fixes. So it's recommended to use our versions when available.

There are other settings which you can toggle:

*

`**max_seq_length = 2048**` – Controls context length. While Llama-3 supports 8192, we recommend 2048 for testing. Unsloth enables 4× longer context fine-tuning.

*

`**dtype = None**` – Defaults to None; use `torch.float16` or `torch.bfloat16` for newer GPUs.

*

`**load_in_4bit = True**` – Enables 4-bit quantization, reducing memory use 4× for fine-tuning. Disabling it enables LoRA 16-bit fine-tuning. You can also enable 16-bit LoRA with `load_in_16bit = True`

*

To enable full fine-tuning (FFT), set `full_finetuning = True`. For 8-bit fine-tuning, set `load_in_8bit = True`.

*

**Note:** Only one training method can be set to `True` at a time.

A common mistake is jumping straight into full fine-tuning (FFT), which is compute-heavy. Start by testing with LoRA or QLoRA first, if it won’t work there, it almost certainly won’t work with FFT. And if LoRA fails, don’t assume FFT will magically fix it.

You can also do [Text-to-speech (TTS)](/docs/basics/text-to-speech-tts-fine-tuning), [reasoning (GRPO)](/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide), [vision](/docs/basics/vision-fine-tuning), [RL](/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide/preference-dpo-orpo-and-kto) (GRPO, DPO), [continued pretraining](/docs/basics/continued-pretraining), text completion and other training methodologies with Unsloth.

Read our guide on choosing models:

[❓What Model Should I Use?](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/what-model-should-i-use)

For inidivudal tutorials on models:

[Complete LLM Directory](/docs/models/tutorials)

## 3. Your Dataset

For LLMs, datasets are collections of data that can be used to train our models. In order to be useful for training, text data needs to be in a format that can be tokenized.

*

You will need to create a dataset usually with 2 columns - question and answer. The quality and amount will largely reflect the end result of your fine-tune so it's imperative to get this part right.

*

You can [synthetically generate data](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/datasets-guide#synthetic-data-generation) and structure your dataset (into QA pairs) using ChatGPT or local LLMs.

*

You can also use our new Synthetic Dataset notebook which automatically parses documents (PDFs, videos etc.), generates QA pairs and auto cleans data using local models like Llama 3.2. [Access the notebook here.](https://colab.research.google.com/github/unslothai/notebooks/blob/main/nb/Meta_Synthetic_Data_Llama3_2_(3B).ipynb)

*

Fine-tuning can learn from an existing repository of documents and continuously expand its knowledge base, but just dumping data alone won’t work as well. For optimal results, curate a well-structured dataset, ideally as question-answer pairs. This enhances learning, understanding, and response accuracy.

*

But, that's not always the case, e.g. if you are fine-tuning a LLM for code, just dumping all your code data can actually enable your model to yield significant performance improvements, even without structured formatting. So it really depends on your use case.

***Read more about creating your dataset:***

[📈Datasets Guide](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/datasets-guide)

For most of our notebook examples, we utilize the [Alpaca dataset](https://docs.unsloth.ai/basics/tutorial-how-to-finetune-llama-3-and-use-in-ollama#id-6.-alpaca-dataset) however other notebooks like Vision will use different datasets which may need images in the answer ouput as well.

### 4. Understand Training Hyperparameters

Learn how to choose the right [hyperparameters](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/lora-hyperparameters-guide) using best practices from research and real-world experiments - and understand how each one affects your model's performance.

**For a complete guide on how hyperparameters affect training, see:**

[🧠Hyperparameters Guide](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/lora-hyperparameters-guide)

## 5. Install + Requirements

You can use Unsloth via two main ways, our free notebooks or locally.

### Unsloth Notebooks

We would recommend beginners to utilise our pre-made [notebooks](/docs/get-started/unsloth-notebooks) first as it's the easiest way to get started with guided steps. You can later export the notebooks to use locally.

Unsloth has step-by-step notebooks for [text-to-speech](/docs/basics/text-to-speech-tts-fine-tuning), [embedding](/docs/basics/embedding-finetuning), GRPO, RL, [vision](/docs/basics/vision-fine-tuning), multimodal, different use-cases and more.

### Local Installation

You can also install Unsloth locally via [Docker](/docs/get-started/install/docker) or `pip install unsloth` (with Linux, WSL or [Windows](/docs/get-started/install/windows-installation)). Also depending on the model you're using, you'll need enough VRAM and resources.

Installing Unsloth will require a Windows or Linux device. Once you install Unsloth, you can copy and paste our notebooks and use them in your own local environment. See:

[🛠️Unsloth Requirements](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-for-beginners/unsloth-requirements)

[📥Installation](/docs/get-started/install)

## 6. Training + Evaluation

Once you have everything set, it's time to train! If something's not working, remember you can always change hyperparameters, your dataset etc.

You’ll see a log of numbers during training. This is the training loss, which shows how well the model is learning from your dataset. For many cases, a loss around 0.5 to 1.0 is a good sign, but it depends on your dataset and task. If the loss is not going down, you might need to adjust your settings. If the loss goes to 0, that could mean overfitting, so it's important to check validation too.

The training loss will appear as numbers

We generally recommend keeping the default settings unless you need longer training or larger batch sizes.

*

`**per_device_train_batch_size = 2**` – Increase for better GPU utilization but beware of slower training due to padding. Instead, increase `gradient_accumulation_steps` for smoother training.

*

`**gradient_accumulation_steps = 4**` – Simulates a larger batch size without increasing memory usage.

*

`**max_steps = 60**` – Speeds up training. For full runs, replace with `num_train_epochs = 1` (1–3 epochs recommended to avoid overfitting).

*

`**learning_rate = 2e-4**` – Lower for slower but more precise fine-tuning. Try values like `1e-4`, `5e-5`, or `2e-5`.

#### Evaluation

In order to evaluate, you could do manually evaluation by just chatting with the model and see if it's to your liking. You can also enable evaluation for Unsloth, but keep in mind it can be time-consuming depending on the dataset size. To speed up evaluation you can: reduce the evaluation dataset size or set `evaluation_steps = 100`.

For testing, you can also take 20% of your training data and use that for testing. If you already used all of the training data, then you have to manually evaluate it. You can also use automatic eval tools but keep in mind that automated tools may not perfectly align with your evaluation criteria.

## 7. Running + Deploying the model

Now let's run the model after we completed the training process! You can edit the yellow underlined part! In fact, because we created a multi turn chatbot, we can now also call the model as if it saw some conversations in the past like below:

Reminder Unsloth itself provides **2x faster inference** natively as well, so always do not forget to call `FastLanguageModel.for_inference(model)`. If you want the model to output longer responses, set `max_new_tokens = 128` to some larger number like 256 or 1024. Notice you will have to wait longer for the result as well!

### Saving + Deployment

For saving and deploying your model in desired inference engines like Ollama, vLLM, Open WebUI, you will need to use the LoRA adapter on top of the base model. We have designated guides for each framework:

[🖥️Inference & Deployment](/docs/basics/inference-and-deployment)

If you’re running inference on a single device (like a laptop or Mac), use llama.cpp to convert to GGUF format to use in Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio etc:

[GGUF & llama.cpp](/docs/basics/inference-and-deployment/saving-to-gguf)

If you’re deploying an LLM for enterprise or multi-user inference for FP8, AWQ, use vLLM:

[vLLM](/docs/basics/inference-and-deployment/vllm-guide)

We can now save the fine-tuned model as a small 100MB file called a LoRA adapter like below. You can instead push to the Hugging Face hub as well if you want to upload your model! Remember to get a Hugging Face [token](https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens) and add your token!

After saving the model, we can again use Unsloth to run the model itself! Use `FastLanguageModel` again to call it for inference!

## 8. We're done!

You've successfully fine-tuned a language model and exported it to your desired inference engine with Unsloth!

To learn more about fine-tuning tips and tricks, head over to our blogs which provide tremendous and educational value: [https://unsloth.ai/blog/](https://unsloth.ai/blog/)

If you need any help on fine-tuning, you can also join our Discord server [here](https://discord.gg/unsloth) or [Reddit r/unsloth](https://www.reddit.com/r/unsloth/). Thanks for reading and hopefully this was helpful!

We have several [notebook examples](/docs/get-started/unsloth-notebooks.md#grpo-reasoning-rl-notebooks), but for most use-cases, standard SFT is sufficient. * **LoRA** is a parameter efficient training method that typically keeps the base model’s weights frozen and trains a small set of added low-rank adapter weights (in 16-bit precision). * **QLoRA** combines LoRA with 4-bit precision to handle very large models with minimal resources. * Unsloth also supports full fine-tuning (FFT) and pretraining, which require significantly more resources, but FFT is usually unnecessary. When done correctly, LoRA can match FFT. * Unsloth **all types models**: [text-to-speech](/docs/basics/text-to-speech-tts-fine-tuning.md), [embedding](/docs/basics/embedding-finetuning.md), GRPO, RL, [vision](/docs/basics/vision-fine-tuning.md), multimodal and more. {% hint style="info" %} Research shows that **training and serving in the same precision** helps preserve accuracy. This means if you want to serve in 4-bit, train in 4-bit and vice versa. {% endhint %} We recommend starting with QLoRA, as it is one of the most accessible and effective methods for training models. Our [dynamic 4-bit](https://unsloth.ai/blog/dynamic-4bit) quants, the accuracy loss for QLoRA compared to LoRA is now largely recovered. You can change the model name to whichever model you like by matching it with model's name on Hugging Face e.g. '`unsloth/llama-3.1-8b-unsloth-bnb-4bit`'. We recommend starting with **Instruct models**, as they allow direct fine-tuning using conversational chat templates (ChatML, ShareGPT etc.) and require less data compared to **Base models** (which uses Alpaca, Vicuna etc). Learn more about the differences between [instruct and base models here](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/what-model-should-i-use.md#instruct-or-base-model). * Model names ending in **`unsloth-bnb-4bit`** indicate they are [**Unsloth dynamic 4-bit**](https://unsloth.ai/blog/dynamic-4bit) **quants**. These models consume slightly more VRAM than standard BitsAndBytes 4-bit models but offer significantly higher accuracy. * If a model name ends with just **`bnb-4bit`**, without "unsloth", it refers to a standard BitsAndBytes 4-bit quantization. * Models with **no suffix** are in their original **16-bit or 8-bit formats**. While they are the original models from the official model creators, we sometimes include important fixes - such as chat template or tokenizer fixes. So it's recommended to use our versions when available. There are other settings which you can toggle: * **`max_seq_length = 2048`** – Controls context length. While Llama-3 supports 8192, we recommend 2048 for testing. Unsloth enables 4× longer context fine-tuning. * **`dtype = None`** – Defaults to None; use `torch.float16` or `torch.bfloat16` for newer GPUs. * **`load_in_4bit = True`** – Enables 4-bit quantization, reducing memory use 4× for fine-tuning. Disabling it enables LoRA 16-bit fine-tuning. You can also enable 16-bit LoRA with `load_in_16bit = True` * To enable full fine-tuning (FFT), set `full_finetuning = True`. For 8-bit fine-tuning, set `load_in_8bit = True`. * **Note:** Only one training method can be set to `True` at a time. {% hint style="info" %} A common mistake is jumping straight into full fine-tuning (FFT), which is compute-heavy. Start by testing with LoRA or QLoRA first, if it won’t work there, it almost certainly won’t work with FFT. And if LoRA fails, don’t assume FFT will magically fix it. {% endhint %} You can also do [Text-to-speech (TTS)](/docs/basics/text-to-speech-tts-fine-tuning.md), [reasoning (GRPO)](/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide.md), [vision](/docs/basics/vision-fine-tuning.md), [RL](/docs/get-started/reinforcement-learning-rl-guide/preference-dpo-orpo-and-kto.md) (GRPO, DPO), [continued pretraining](/docs/basics/continued-pretraining.md), text completion and other training methodologies with Unsloth. {% columns %} {% column %} Read our guide on choosing models: {% content-ref url="/pages/BSShKhLoFNlGWO5cN8VJ" %} [What Model Should I Use?](/docs/get-started/fine-tuning-llms-guide/what-model-should-i-use.md) {% endcontent-ref %} {% endcolumn %} {% column %} For inidivudal tutorials on models: {% content-ref url="/pages/BAeSP6aOxvSeDUzCgKOK" %} [Complete LLM Directory](/docs/models/tutorials.md) {% endcontent-ref %} {% endcolumn %} {% endcolumns %} ## 3. Training + Evaluation Once you have everything set, it's time to train! If something's not working, remember you can always change hyperparameters, your dataset etc. You’ll see a log of numbers during training. This is the training loss, which shows how well the model is learning from your dataset. For many cases, a loss around 0.5 to 1.0 is a good sign, but it depends on your dataset and task. If the loss is not going down, you might need to adjust your settings. If the loss goes to 0, that could mean overfitting, so it's important to check validation too. We generally recommend keeping the default settings unless you need longer training or larger batch sizes. * **`per_device_train_batch_size = 2`** – Increase for better GPU utilization but beware of slower training due to padding. Instead, increase `gradient_accumulation_steps` for smoother training. * **`gradient_accumulation_steps = 4`** – Simulates a larger batch size without increasing memory usage. * **`max_steps = 60`** – Speeds up training. For full runs, replace with `num_train_epochs = 1` (1–3 epochs recommended to avoid overfitting). * **`learning_rate = 2e-4`** – Lower for slower but more precise fine-tuning. Try values like `1e-4`, `5e-5`, or `2e-5`. #### Evaluation In order to evaluate, you could do manually evaluation by just chatting with the model and see if it's to your liking. You can also enable evaluation for Unsloth, but keep in mind it can be time-consuming depending on the dataset size. To speed up evaluation you can: reduce the evaluation dataset size or set `evaluation_steps = 100`. For testing, you can also take 20% of your training data and use that for testing. If you already used all of the training data, then you have to manually evaluate it. You can also use automatic eval tools but keep in mind that automated tools may not perfectly align with your evaluation criteria. ## 7.
